speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to some optimistic indicators which encourage optimism and suggest that the national Government has been pursuing proper and prudent policies. First, inflation has fallen to an annual rate of only 8.3 per cent as of today. Housing starts are up from a low of
86,000	in September, 1982, to 165,000 last month, a 90 per cent increase. Sales of passenger cars increased 37 per cent between July and December of 1982.
The Conference Board of Canada's index of consumer confidence rose 36 per cent, from 54.8 per cent in the second quarter of 1982 to 74.7 per cent in the fourth quarter of 1982.
Senior business executives have become more optimistic about the near-term prospects for the Canadian economy. According to the Conference Board survey of business, attitudes and confidence in Canada's investment climate have also improved.
Pension funds in 1982 showed a sharp improvement over 1981, according to private surveys. Equity funds have increased 39.1 per cent over the past six months.
Finally, the Toronto Stock Exchange 300 composite has risen from about 1850 in mid-December to 2150 in the past week.
A large part of the credit for this improvement should go to the Government, which has addressed the economic situation through hard work and constructive policy initiatives. This is in contrast to those in the Official Opposition whose negativism and lack of policies are destroying their Party from within.

subsubtopic: POLAND-IMPRISONMENT OF SOLIDARITY HUSBAND AND WIFE ACTIVISTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday in Warsaw, Zbigniew Romaszewski of the
Polish Solidarity Movement was sentenced to four and a half years in prison by a military court for activities which, in any other country, would be considered legitimate in defence of the freedom of information and expression. His wife, Zofia, was sentenced to three years in prison at the same time.
This is what the military regime is doing in Poland, seeking to extinguish those flickers of freedom that Solidarity has been struggling to keep alight. When will the Government protest? Is it making excessive demands to speak out about what is happening and carrying information to others?
Are Romaszewski and his wife guilty of making excessive demands which our Canadian Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) hoped the military regime in Poland could keep Solidarity from making? On December 18, 1981, only five days after the steel curtain of martial law had descended upon Poland, Canada's Prime Minister said:
Hopefully the military regime will be able not only to keep Solidarity from making excessive demands-
The record of the Government in verbal support of freedoms throughout the world, at Helsinki, for example, and Madrid, is not matched by its diplomatic protests when specific incidents of suppression of freedom occur, as they are occurring today in Poland.

Madam Speaker, women have not achieved equality in Canada. In October, 1981, the NDP asked the Government to establish a Standing Committee on the Status of Women. Unfortunately the Minister responsible for the Status of Women did not support this request. Since then, the economic situation for women has drastically deteriorated, while many more women are left alone to raise children and to face unemployment and poverty as they grow older.
We are pleased that the slow learner Conservatives have finally supported our request which we recently reintroduced to House Leaders. Because 52 per cent of our population remains disadvantaged, it is essential that there be one standing committee which will monitor all legislation affecting

February 18, 1983
women, including the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and which will receive annual reports from all Government Departments concerned with women's programs, and undertake special projects to benefit women.
The Government and the Minister responsible give lip service to equality, yet they have not even implemented the 1970 recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. There has been no increase in daycare. The wage gap has widened. Government restraint has worsened economic hardship. Government action on pension reform has been shelved. The Government has refused mandatory affirmative action.
To begin to right these wrongs, the Government must agree to establish a Standing Committee on the status of women as a priority for parliamentary reform.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under Standing Order 21 I rise to encourage the Government to continue to develop positive and constructive policies aimed at achieving energy security at a fair price for Canadians.
Three years ago the Government pledged to establish a "made in Canada" blended price for oil, resulting in lower costs to Canadian consumers.
I further urge the Government to continue progress on such projects as the Nova Scotia offshore, the synthetic crude refinery and benzene plant at Scotford, Alberta, and the Beaufort Sea exploration. The Government, in the absence of any specific and constructive suggestions from the Opposition, should continue to encourage economic development through initiatives, such as the Office of Industrial and Regional Benefit, to ensure that the Canadian industrial and manufacturing benefits from these projects are maximized.
Finally, I urge the Government to encourage the creation of jobs in different regions by ensuring that energy maintains its central position in the Government's approach to industrial and regional development, giving Canadian industry a price advantage by keeping costs low.

Madam Speaker, we are on the verge of entering the fourth year of this first session of the 32nd Parliament. It is unprecedented in Canadian history. As we look back we see three years of fumbling, blumbing, Government intervention and interference, broken promises, helter skelter policies and, for most Canadians, dissipated
illusions, shattered confidence, and broken hopes and dreams. The Government has not only fractured the parliamentary system but has broken faith with the Canadian people. Canadians say that they have had enough. As the Board of Dromore might say,
Pierre, you're nimble; Pierre, you're quick.
But you, and your manoeuvrings, make us sick.
Oh, Oh!

subsubtopic: CONDEMNATION OF QUEBEC'S SUSPENSION OF RIGHTS CHARTER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to express my concern and the concern of my Party over the vicious attacks that have been made against working people in this country over the last few months, and to express our belief that it is not working people who are responsible for the problems of Canada.
The federal Liberal Government began these attacks a few months ago with its six and five program which broke the contracts of workers and stole money from pensioners. The Conservative Government of Ontario, which had already shown itself ready to use its full power against hospital orderlies but not even to pressure doctors, was quick to follow the federal Government.
The most drastic, vicious and immoral attack on working people, however, has come from the Government of Quebec.
In its recent legislation it even had to suspend its own Charter of Rights which is supposed to provide basic mini-mums of freedoms to citizens in a democracy.
Like the federal Government, it broke contracts and stole money, perhaps showing Rene Levesque's Liberal roots. But it went further and threatened firings and slashes in seniority and pensions. Such cuts in seniority will most hurt union militants who may then be laid off because of lack of seniority. Such moves are union bashing in its most vicious form.
The Government of Quebec has absolutely refused to bargain in good faith with its workers. We would now like to call on the Government of Quebec to restore collective bargaining and to bargain with its workers, treating them as citizens in a democracy rather than as scapegoats to be attacked for the Government's convenience.

Interest rates are now at their lowest level in five years, and of course lower than at any point during the Clark Government, and the downward trend continues. The cost of living index dropped to 8.3 per cent in January and, over the past six months, has only been increasing at an average annual rate of 4.2 per cent. The previous six months it had been increasing at an average annual rate of 12.5 per cent.
Non-COLA wage settlements were down to 7.3 per cent in the fourth quarter of 1982, a drop of 50 per cent from a year earlier. Surely that is evidence that the six and five program is in fact working.

subsubtopic: CAPE BRETON COAL AGREEMENT-ROLE OF DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister who in April, 1980, sent his Minister a set of guidelines for their behaviour. If I may quote to the Prime Minister one of his guidelines:
In any official dealings with former office holders, Ministers must ensure that they do not provide grounds or the appearance of grounds for allegations of improper influence, privileged access or preferential treatment.
My question to the Prime Minister is this. Has he determined whether the Deputy Prime Minister, when he participated in a press conference in April, 1981, to announce the Scotia Coal Synfuels Plant, was aware of those guidelines? Also, has he determined, if the Deputy Prime Minister was so aware, why he felt it was reasonable to breach those guidelines that day?

subsubtopic: MR. HERBERT-RECORDING OF ADMITTANCE TO AND DEPARTURE FROM PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question of privilege deals directly with the right of a Member of Parliament to have free and unimpeded access to his or her office at any and all hours of the day and night and not be subjected to any recording of his or her comings or goings.
Last evening, after ten years of free access to my office in the Confederation Building, I was stopped and asked for identification. This in itself is not an issue, although there were somewhat humiliating aspects in that it was carried out in front of other employees who have been aware of my identity for the last decade.
My privilege was, in my opinion, violated when my name was recorded on a list. Inquiries elicited the information that my entry and exit to my office was to be recorded on each and every occasion after 7.30 in the evening. As Your Honour is aware, our committee activities, which are an integral part of our work here on Parliament Hill, continue until ten o'clock p.m. and sometimes later. Whatever security measures may be felt necessary should not apply solely during our evening work period, as if such work times differred from any other time during the day.
Of additional concern is the use to which such lists can be put if they fall into the wrong hands since there is no verification of their authenticity. Quite apparently, since an Hon. Member is not asked to sign in and out, an identity mistake can be made which might not bother anybody in the private sector but which could have considerable influence on the assessment of the conduct of an Hon. Member by his constituents.
Personally, I consider the recording of the times of entry and exit of an Hon. Member in and out of his or her office during regular working hours to be an invasion of his or her privacy and a practice fraught with abuse which could have a direct influence on the election of the people's representatives.
On the assumption, Madam Speaker, that you recognize that I do have a question of privilege, may I suggest that you take the matter under advisement. May I further suggest that, at least during the interim period, no records be kept of the movement of MPs between the hours of seven o'clock a.m. and eleven o'clock p.m. on weekdays.

subsubtopic: MR. HERBERT-RECORDING OF ADMITTANCE TO AND DEPARTURE FROM PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. HERBERT-RECORDING OF ADMITTANCE TO AND DEPARTURE FROM PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS
speechtext: First, I do not believe that this is a question of privilege; it concerns administrative decisions. I would welcome a discussion in my office with either the Hon. Member or the representatives of the different Parties.

subsubtopic: MR. HERBERT-RECORDING OF ADMITTANCE TO AND DEPARTURE FROM PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS
speechtext: It certainly is privilege.

speechtext:
I want to say to the Hon. Member that the presence of anyone in the buildings which we call the House of Commons is recorded and has been recorded for a long time. These records are kept in order to ascertain who is in the
buildings and how many people are in the buildings for security and fire reasons. We have always kept a record of the number of people who were in the buildings, expecially after hours, because one must assume that most people have left their offices by that time.
As for the Hon. Member being required to sign his name, I am sure that was a mistake. Members of Parliament should not be required to sign their names when they go in and out of the buildings, because the guards are trained to recognize Hon. Members. Perhaps the Hon. Member was unlucky and had to deal with one of the guards who happened to be new or simply did not recognize him. It is quite clear that Hon. Members do not have to sign in and out of their offices. Other people who enter the buildings will be required to sign.
Concerning the records, I can assure Hon. Members that those records are not kept on our files forever. They are automatically destroyed. They are simply kept for the purpose of knowing who is in the buildings on a particular day for fire and security reasons.

speechtext:
Joining in the discussion on that particular point, may I indicate that on many occasions it is impossible for the security staff to ascertain who is in the building or who is leaving the building. There are many social occasions when people are going in and out of the buildings between ten-thirty o'clock p.m. and eleven-thirty o'clock p.m. There is no record being kept at that time, nor has there been a record kept, as to who is going in or out, be it stranger, employee, officer of the House, Member of Parliament or Senator.
I would suggest that this is an administrative matter, as Your Honour said. The rules state that administrative matters are to stand referred to the Members' Services Committee. Since Members and their privileges are being affected, I find it strange indeed that this matter was not referred to the Committee for consideration before action was taken.

speechtext: What is the over-all cost of the annual "farm enumerative survey" that is done by Statistics Canada and what is the information gathered used for?

Statistics Canada reports:
The Farm Enumerative Survey is a general purpose annual survey conducted in the designated Canadian Wheat Board area at an estimated cost of $1.1 million for the fiscal year 1982/83. The statistics produced from the survey are used for many different purposes. Expenditure and acreage data provide a major portion of the data used in the calculation of payouts under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. Farm expenditure estimates are also used in calculation of net farm income which, in turn, is part of the calculation of Canada's national income. In addition, data related to farm crop production are used by farmers, farmer co-operatives and such agencies as the Canadian Wheat Board in planning crop production and marketing strategies.
Livestock information from the survey provides an indication of the future supply of animals and animal products. All segments of the agriculture and related industries are thus provided with unbiased information to be used in planning their production and marketing activities.
Finally, all Farm Enumerative Survey data are of relevance to federal and provincial Departments of Agriculture in the development and management of policies and programs aimed at the food and agriculture sector.

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
speechtext:
That, in light of the Government's outright betrayal of the Canadian people and its repudiation of its 1980 election promises to reduce unemployment, combat inflation, avoid inflationary tax hikes and excessive energy price increases, reduce the deficit, and implement an industrial strategy for Canada, this House calls upon the Government to face its responsibility to Canadians and take immediate action to live up to the commitments that it made in 1980 or resign.
He said: Madam Speaker, today is a tragic anniversary in the history of this country. In the words of President Roosevelt after Pearl Harbour: "This is a day that will live in infamy". I refer, of course, to February 18, 1980, the day on which this Government was elected to office. It was a day which inaugurated the most dismal and disastrous three years in the history of our country.
Three years ago today, a country that was prosperous, a country that was buoyant, a country that was full of hope and promise, started on the long, downward path of Liberal Government despair, ineptitude and disaster. Canadians who were gainfully employed three years ago are now walking the streets. Firms that were prosperous three years ago and that
February 18, 1983

had some hope are now in the bankruptcy courts. The pleasant, smiling countryside with its prosperous farms is now rapidly becoming deserted and full of despair, due to the mismanagement of the Liberal Government sitting opposite.
Young people have been forced out of their homes; others have seen their hopes of security blasted and torn asunder. Older people have seen the Government renege and cut back on their hopes of a worry-free old age, paid for with their own contributions. Not even the widowed mother or orphan has been spared by a Government which spends without stint to realize its own peculiar centralist and socialist objectives, and passes on the bill to Canadians without explanation or without apology.
One must go back to the 1940s to equal the distress and uneasiness which prevails in the economy today. This country has been run headlong into an economic crisis of the first magnitude, due largely to the mismanagement and incompetence of this Government. Brief after brief after brief, from both labour and management, have made it clear that the economy has been staggered by a series of rude shocks deriving from this Government's policies or lack of action.
Nothing is so urgent in the minds of millions of Canadians who have been made to suffer because of this Government's indifference and neglect as to remove this Government from office. Incompetent, inept, untrustworthy, careless in its corruption and heartless in its approach to the problems, this Government has lost the confidence of the Canadian people.
Hear, hear!

One after another, its policies have proven to be exactly the wrong remedies at the wrong time. From FIRA to the NEP, from the CIDC to Canagrex, they have turned out to be incredibly costly, cumbersome and destructive.
Trust remains a major ingredient in human affairs. Trust has departed from this Government. Canadians do not trust this Government. Foreign countries do not trust this Government. Our friends and allies do not trust this Government.
Yesterday we had one of those little vest pocket lectures which spring so readily to the lips of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whenever he is in trouble. Like the squid of the underseas caverns, he retreats first this way, then that way, emitting an opaque cloud in order to befog the issue.
It is hard to believe that a man of the Prime Minister's intelligence fails to understand that when two Ministers sign a contract providing monetary gain to a former Cabinet colleague, that conduct is not condoned in any code of ethics in the world from the Code of Hammurabi to the Judeo-Chris-tian ethic.
I come now to the shabby record of broken Liberal election promises. It is a shocking spectacle, Mr. Speaker. It is the record of a Government which over and over, blatantly and furiously, broke its word to those Canadians who had accepted on trust its sparkling promises, promises about full employment; promises about an industrial strategy; promises about a buoyant economy! Promises! Promises! Promises!
Supply
Here was a Government and Party which promised, in the words of one of their former crystal ball-gazing leaders, "A new heaven and a new earth". Nothing was sacred to this Party and to that Prime Minister. In election after election they promised a brighter world and a nobler future. They promised megaprojects. They promised high technology. They promised something for the aged, something for youth, something for the newly married, something for students, something for the scientists and something for the farmers. Those promises now read like a litany of broken dreams.
As Canadians contemplate the wreckage of those bright dreams-the farm foreclosures, the abolition of the Crow rate, the monopolistic food marketing policy of Canagrex, the sprawling empire of Crown corporations responsible to no one but the Prime Minister, the bankruptcies, the unemployment, the incredible expenditures, the demand on Parliament for blank cheques-they can only ask themselves whether they are dreaming.
When I was a young boy I read Robert Louis Stevenson's book "The Wrecker". Members will recall in that book that a group of unprincipled individuals lit bonfires on the beach to lure ships on to the shore so that the sailors could be massacred and their property plundered. That is what Canadians must be thinking of today when reflecting back on the lure of the promises of 1980 and what they are getting today.
Hear, hear!

No Government in the history of any free Western nation with a parliamentary tradition has ever been so irresponsible or so reckless. No Government has so quickly lost the trust of the people, the confidence of investors and the friendship of our neighbours and allies. The reason is that this Government is totally unpredictable. The only predictable thing about it is that if there is any way of screwing up things, it will do it.
Hear, hear!

I say that with my usual good feeling. What did they say in 1980? They were going to establish a petroleum pricing and auditing agency. They were going to construct a reversible pipeline to the Province of Quebec. Somewhere along the line that got reversed. The Government's share of increased oil prices through PetroCan would go to the poorer regions of Canada. I presume those are the regions where "Dire Straits" is located.
They were going to boost alternate energy through an alternate energy corporation. That would take in wind, sun, tidal power, biomass and liquid coal. Well, the last one proved a bonanza for at least one former Minister. As for the wind, they have not harnessed it yet, except here in the House every time they speak. As for the sun, it is still shining in spite of them. It is the only thing left in this country that is free.
On January 17, 1980 the Prime Minister promised to double track the CNR. He must have been serious. He is still

February 18, 1983
Supply
promising to double track the CNR. On January 10 the Prime Minister said the Liberal Party would provide hundreds of thousands of jobs. They did that. The only hitch was that the jobs were in Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong and West Germany.
He said we would expand FIRA so that Canadians would control the economy. FIRA helped the economy like the earthquake helped San Francisco. He said he would set up an international trading company. Probably this would follow along the lines of similar state corporations in the Soviet Union and the satellite states. They have not done this yet because is still some of the domestic economy they have not finished wrecking.
The industrial strategy would encourage workers to become shareholders in the firms in which they work. They should have followed through on that one. So many firms went bankrupt, nobody wanted them but the workers.
There are some relevant quotations from the Prime Minister. They do not have quite the ring of Chairman Mao nor the predictability factor of Nostradamus, but for the student of broken promises they are not without a certain macabre interest. In Toronto on January 12, 1980 the Prime Minister said:
This Party will not simply stand by and let the recession come.
No. They brought it on.
We will fight it and overcome it.
The Prime Minister in his own personal Pilgrim's Progress was ready to wrestle anything, anywhere, any time. He would wrestle inflation to the ground. He would fight and overcome. He did this by the simple expedient of jumping into the 707 and taking off. In January, 1980 the Prime Minister said:
We have an economic program for the eighties which will enhance dignity, create opportunity and provide security.
It did just that, but the people it reached were few in number. They were all either in the Cabinet or were ex-Cabinet Ministers. In February, 1980 in Toronto the Prime Minister really got off a bomb:
I would want to manage the economy in such a way that interest rates would in fact come down-
Then there was the famous statement by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), who said on CITY-TV on February 7, 1980 that he would resign his seat if interest rates did not come down. Somehow, as time went on, his seat became more precious than his own personal integrity.
Then we had the Prime Minister's personal formula. He said:
We would bring interest rates down by fighting inflation, not by manipulating the dollar.
So much for bright words tarnished by subsequent events. The Prime Minister got off some gems in January, 1980 when he said:
The deficit will be reduced in a phased and orderly fashion.
We will not add to the deficit by adding new programs.
As the poet said:
Words, words, words, I know not what they mean.
We are at a point now where this whole nation has expressed a total lack of confidence in this Government. We are at a point now where this whole nation wants them to go. Consumer confidence has dwindled away. Business and industry are consumed by uneasiness and uncertainty. Investor confidence has plummeted to zero.
At the present time the most serious impediment to the recovery of our economy is the presence of this Government. The single most constructive act which this Government could perform in the best interests of this country would be to resign and give Canadians back their inalienable right to elect a Government of their choice.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to follow the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Nielsen) in discussing this very serious questions and very serious motion.
Three years ago the Liberal Party perpetrated the greatest electoral fraud in Canada's history. After an election campaign in which every possible deceitful promise was made to the Canadian people, that tired old gang took over again. Today we want to examine in the House some of the promises made to the Canadian people by this fraudulent gang of thugs and bring them forward for the Canadian people to examine once again.
On February 9, 1980, they said that a new Liberal Government will work to reduce unemployment through a program of responsible fiscal and monetary management. What happened? In January, 1983 a record 1.6 million Canadians were out of work with a net loss of 578,000 jobs between August, 1981 and January, 1983. The unemployment rate in January, 1983 was 12.4 per cent compared to an unemployment rate in January, 1980 of 7.6 per cent; and according to the Economic Council, the unemployment rate will be in excess of 10 per cent for the next five years.
Unemployment Insurance benefits in 1982 were equal to $8.5 billion, more than the combined Government spending of the four Atlantic Provinces.
But more serious than the 1.6 million Canadians who do not have a job, Mr. Speaker, are the 500,000 Canadians who are so discouraged that they have given up looking for work, and the 390,000 Canadians who are not working to their full capacity. That is a situation which just cannot be allowed to continue in this country. Forty-eight per cent more workers are unemployed now than in 1979. In the past, unemployment has risen because the number of jobs has not increased as fast as the labour force. Today, unemployment is rising because jobs are simply disappearing. The year 1982 was the first time in a quarter of a century that we had a year-over-year decline in the number of jobs.
February 18, 1983

In my riding of Simcoe North, the number of people employed in the service and manufacturing sectors has fallen by 16 per cent since that election of 1980. It is bad in the Orillia area, which I just referred to, but it is even worse in Midland and Penetanguishene where there is an unemployment rate of 33 per cent, which is a result of the failure of this Government to live up to any of their promises. Midland and Penetanguishene had ten manufacturing plants completely shut down. RCA, with 1,220 employees, is shut down completely. We went to see the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce in the summer of 1982 and he promised help in arranging for the sale of this plant, but he has done nothing. The Liberal Government has done nothing to help RCA and those 1,220 Canadians who want to work. It failed them completely. That is the legacy of the 1980 election promises for the riding of Simcoe North.
This Government said: "We will not simply stand by and let the recession come; we will fight it and we will overcome it". That is a quote from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in January, 1980. But, Mr. Speaker, they did not fight it. They did not overcome it. They did everything possible to bring on the recession. That promise was kept in reverse. The Government brought on the recession which Canadians are now fighting.
One of the favourite tactics of this wasted front bench of the Liberal Party is to attribute the poor state of our economy to international factors. Let us deal with some of those international factors. In the United States the GNP has dropped by only 1.9 from its peak in the third quarter. In Canada it has dropped 6.9 per cent. Why do we have to drop that much farther and that much faster than the United States if we are linked to them, as they say? Industrial production in the United States dropped 11.5 per cent by October of last year from a high level, while in Canada the corresponding figure was 18.8 per cent. I ask the Liberal Government again, why does industrial production have to drop so much faster and harder in Canada than the United States if it is an international situation?
Manufacturers in Canada reported in the third quarter that they were operating at the lowest level of their capacity since records were first kept in 1961. I ask Hon. Members opposite, did they promise that they were going to have that effect on the manufacturers of Canada, on the production, and on the jobs which have been lost as a direct result of their inaction, ineptness and lack of caring for anyone who works in this country?
Let me talk about the famous Liberal energy policy. They said: "The Liberal price hike will be less than half of what the Tories plan to inflict on you; we will negotiate an increase of less than 14 cents". That may sound like a specious comment out of the comic section of the newspapers, but it is not, Mr. Speaker. It is a comment made by the present Prime Minister. This is by far the most often broken promise of the Liberal Government. Gasoline prices, which were promised to rise only
Supply
14 cents, have gone up 17 times. The price of OPEC oil is going down but Canadian prices are continuing to go up.
The Government did not promise exactly the kind of national energy policy we got, but we got one all right. Canadians got a national energy policy and, brother, did it do something for us. The Government's energy policy resulted in oil rigs leaving Alberta and the cancellation of the Alsands project, which would have meant jobs for hundreds of thousands of Canadians; the cancellation of the Cold Lake project; the loss of the spin-off benefits, not just for Alberta where the oil is in the ground, or British Columbia or Saskatchewan, but for Ontario. We in this Party happen to believe that the energy policy is something which should benefit all Canadians, not from a price standpoint so much as from a job standpoint, because those jobs which could have been there for us in the energy industry are in all Provinces. That is what this Government neglects to consider when it looks at the electoral map and sees there are no seats there for it in Alberta, so it just does not care. In the meantime, it inflicts pain and misery on the entire country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: If it is not true, you tell me where the jobs went.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, you love Alberta. That kind of love anyone can do without, thank you very much.
I would like to refer to my riding once again. In my riding of Simcoe North, we wanted the megaprojects to go ahead because we have industries that supply the energy industries. We have Fahramet, a company in my riding which produces refractor tubes used in the energy industry. But what happened? As a result of the Liberal national energy policy, it went on work sharing. It cut back on its staff. That is the result in my riding of what the Liberal Government has done about energy prices.
In Canada we now have a $27.36 billion, or whatever it is today, deficit as a result of the mismanagement of the Liberal Government and its failure to keep its promises. We have an interest burden. Interest on our national debt is $700 for every man, woman and child in Canada. That is $1,700 per year per taxpayer. The interest on the debt in 1982-83 equalled 4.8 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product. When the present Prime Minister took office it was 2 per cent.
This country, as a result of mismanagement of the economy by the Liberal Government, has lost its fiscal flexibility. In 1968-69 one tax dollar in nine was needed to service our debt. Today, one tax dollar in three services our debt. As a result of the massive Government borrowing the private sector interest rates go up.
Lastly, when we talk about the deficit we talk about the confidence which people have in the country. The confidence in this Government, Mr. Speaker, is absolutely gone. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) this week had the nerve to ask us (a) to let him introduce a Bill without any financial information, a Bill to borrow money; and (b), without any

February 18, 1983
Supply
notice to go ahead and introduce his Bill so he could borrow some $19 billion. Both Parties on this side, Mr. Speaker, have rejected that offer because he comes forward with no financial statements, no projections. Oh, yes, he has offered us projections to March 31, and I would venture to say that, given that the Minister of Finance has only six weeks in which to goof on those predictions, probably his prediction for this year is as close as any prediction any Minister of Finance in that Government has ever made. That is not saying very much, but we are saying it because he has only six weeks to goof, so that is probably going to be the closest prediction. But once again, it is a broken promise to the people of Canada who put that tawdry group in office on the basis of their election promises.
I have a minute or two, Mr. Speaker, and I want to talk about bankruptcies. Just what has happened to the Canadian economy as a result of the Liberal Government's inept handling of the financial situation in this country? Personal bankruptcies have climbed. There has been a 46 per cent increase in the number of personal bankruptcies since 1980,- thanks to the way this Government has handled the country's affairs. Those bankruptcies cover the manufacturing section, construction section, all areas of the economic sector, all as a result of the failure of this Government to do anything about the economy.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I say that this Government has made promise after promise which it will be reminded of over the next few months and in the next election. There is no question but that it is going to be with a heavy heart that every Member on that side seeks re-election if he or she has the nerve to go back to the people and say: "Yes, I am the candidate who promised you lower energy prices. I am the Member of Parliament who sat here from February, 1980 and watched interest rates skyrocket, bankruptcies climb, watched foreclosures and powers of sale. I am the Member of Parliament that you could not get hold of when all those problems were occurring. But I am back here and I am promising once again to give you all of those things." I tell you, Mr. Speaker, and I tell the Members of the House on the opposite side: this time it will not wash.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of State (Finance)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I count myself fortunate to have the opportunity to enter this debate on the third anniversary of the election of this Government on February 18, 1980. It was my intention to take some time to comment on the constructive alternatives and policies that the mover of the motion, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Nielsen), put in his remarks to support his criticism contained in the motion. However, I am somewhat taken off guard because, if you review his speech and the speech of the Hon. Member who has just spoken, there is, of course, not one single sentence with one single idea, one single constructive criticism, offered by the Opposition. Therefore, I am really caught short because I have nothing positive or constructive to respond to in the comments of the speakers thus far.
It is important in any government, in any mandate, to reflect on what I perceive as being some very high points and, indeed, some very low points in my experience, which in this Parliament has been exactly three years. My election to this House for the first time, therefore, was on February 18, 1980. I found myself fortunate to have been part of this Parliament which after a long time finally adopted, and is in the process of implementing, a constructive, comprehensive national program for the development and protection of the energy resources that are so important to all Canadians.
History will recall no doubt that in this century the initiative taken by the Government, given a mandate by the people of Canada on February 18, 1980, will go down as one of the most important economic initiatives of any Government at any time. The first objective of the plan, to secure adequate supply for future generations, has been achieved. The second objective was to achieve that at a fair price, and that has been accomplished.
The Opposition are critical, in part, of some of the pricing policies of the Government but they did not indicate that their policy, as I understand it, is to charge a price at least 10 per cent higher than that which prevails under the National Energy Program. Indeed, some Members of the Party opposite have argued that the price should be even higher than world price, that we should lead in soaking Canadians in the area of pricing. We have not heard any policy from the Conservative Party but I have perceived this from public statements by individual Members of that Party.
That was a high point of the last three years of this Government of Canada. Probably equally important and certainly as important and fulfilling to me was the opportunity to be part of a Government that was responsible for patriation of the legal framework of this country and the return of the Constitution. More important in that process was the granting to all Canadians in future of the Charter of Human Rights, which is second to hone in the world. Those words come from the Leader of the New Democratic Party. The Charter grants rights and protections for every Canadian from coast to coast into the future, and it is second to none in the world. For me it has been a thrill to be part of this Parliament and of the
Supply
process that resulted in that achievement. It is no mean achievement by this Parliament.
I was in the Chamber on the evening that the results of the referendum in the Province of Quebec were announced. That referendum was the springboard in the energy and activity that resulted in the return of the Constitution. I was here when we received the information that the majority of people in that part of Canada said they were Canadians first. Following that, all Canadians through their representatives, federal and provincial, joined in seeking the return of the Constitution to give us a basis from which to address the future, not as it affects the individual Canadian through the Charter of Rights but through the representatives of federal and provincial Governments, and to proceed to the next challenge. That is the continuing and most important challenge of this Parliament, the achievement of economic recovery in the country and the formation of an economic base that will emerge hand in hand with the legal and social services that have been achieved through the Charter of Rights.
The third and equally important highlight is my small role as a Member of this Government and of this Party in signalling to the Canadian people that this Parliament would address leadership in the process of economic recovery. We did that by signaling to Canadians that restraint was important. I knew that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and senior Ministers of the Government have, through intergovernmental meetings, attempted to draw the support of the Provinces. I think of their meeting in January or February, 1982 on the restraint program.
Unfortunately, I suppose, it was a little too soon. When the Government found out it could not carry the support of the Provinces, it introduced a program of restraint in the budget of 1982. At that time it adopted a restraint program which applied, first of all, to Members of this House, to Members of the other place, to those who assist this House, this Government, agencies of the Government and any agency that has contact with the Government. We said that restraint would have to be one of the first steps in a long program of economic recovery. The program has been dubbed the six and five program. On the initiative of this Government and supported by the Official Opposition, it was felt that that was the place to start economic recovery, to show that if we had any excess of financial ability it should be used in productive ways and that other people should be willing to make sacrifices. We started that program in the House of Commons. I predict that in years to come it will be identified as a very significant start on a program of economic recovery in the country.
Like all industrial countries and like all developing countries in the last few years, we have reached a watershed. The old economies do not work and the old systems are creaking. The world economies have reached a watershed. We know the challenge of this country and other industrialized countries as well as the developing countries is to establish a new restructuring. Better ways must be found to make the economies work.

In summary, Mr. Speaker, those are the high points to me. I count myself privileged to have been a Member of the House involved in these very important initiatives and to be a Member of the Government with some input into the decisions and leadership demonstrated in this short three-year period.
There were also low points, Mr. Speaker. I will not dwell on them because the Opposition has spent the last 45 minutes painting an unconstructive, doomsday scenario. You would not think that anything was possible or that there was any hope for Canadians if you believed that doomsday scenario.
I offer this observation on the low point in the hope that it might be instructive and constructive. I compare the operation of this House and its federal system of government with my personal experience in municipal government in Metropolitan Toronto. As Mayor of the borough of Scarborough and a member of the Metropolitan Toronto Council, I found that we addressed problems quickly. I suppose it is the nature of the animal that the system of local government seems to be able to respond more quickly than the federal Government. I cannot describe the depth of frustration, for example, in watching this House take six months to attempt to get $300 million of assistance for the housing industry while I was housing Minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. When the House rose at one o'clock, the Hon. Minister of State for Finance had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment of the House for the lunch period, I was reminding Hon. Members and those observing the debate in the House of Commons today that February 18, 1980 was the initiation of this Government and that we were at the three-year anniversary of the mandate of the Government. Also I indicated that, in my view, this Thirty-second Parliament of Canada would be recorded as one of the most productive and significant in the history of all Parliaments of Canada.
I did that, drawing to mind three initiatives taken by the Government. The first was the securing of energy resources for Canadians in the future, brought under the control of all Canadians at a price which was affordable and which was 10 per cent less than the price of the Official Opposition, in a national program which is successful, even at this point of our mandate, and beyond our expectation of achieving conservation by Canadians in energy at a rate and degree we did not think would be possible when we began the program.
Second, this Parliament will be remembered because Canada received its own constitutional ability, with Governments sharing power in the country, to make agreements in the future as to how legal structures and laws will be amended to suit Canadians. Of course, a major component of repatriation was the inclusion of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, described by the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) as the best Charter of Rights in the whole world.
Finally, the Government is in the process of addressing economic recovery. I reminded Hon. Members that the First step was the issue of restraint. We felt that all sectors of the Canadian economy and its people, but more important this House and we as Members, had to demonstrate leadership in the area of restraint, and we did that. The six and five program, as it has come to be known, was supported in the House by the largest majority of Members, including the Tory Party and the Liberal Government. The program was a start toward bringing some realism to the recovery of the economy which for Canada, being a trading country, was very important. I am referring to the issues upon which everyone reflects these days-the issue of productivity and the issue of the efficiency of our economy to compete with world markets.
I concluded my remarks by indicating that my experience was previously in municipal politics and by comparing it with the way in which the federal Government and the Parliament of Canada operate. Unhappily, the comparison was a disappointment. I have been a Member of the House for exactly three years. I have been disappointed by the slowness of the House in addressing economic problems in Canada. -and that this House further recognizes the failure of Her Majesty's Official Loyal Opposition to fulfil its responsibilities in this Parliament and recognizes that when its members formed the Government in the Thirty-first Parliament, they broke as many promises as the present Government, but in a shorter period of time. We have a population in this country now who has no confidence in the Liberal Party as a result of the long historical trend in its behaviour. They have no confidence in the Prime Minister and they have no confidence that that group respects this Parliament. That is a very serious situation.

problems that we have had in this House, where one group says: "In the last election we got crucified for making commitments, and therefore we will make no commitments to the Canadian people; we will concentrate on eroding the confidence of Canadians in the people who govern this country". Had they done that, that would have acted as a lever to move the Government, but their only position was that there is too much UFFI and it is the Liberals' fault. They refused to put forward a position.
That has also happened on the bail-out of Dome. The Leader of the Official Opposition said that he did not know what they should do, that they should probably refer it to a parliamentary committee. That was another cop-out.
The Conservative Party as the Official Opposition in this Parliament has failed miserably in its responsibility to the Canadian people to put forward alternatives. There are certain questions of moral responsibility, of appropriate activity for Cabinet Ministers, that are certainly valid questions in this House; but there is a tendency on the part of some people to see it boil over into character assassination for long-term political gain, rather than to clarify what is appropriate behaviour in this House and establish relevant, pertinent guidelines for conduct. That should be the end result of the current exercise.

rational budget. It was probably not just the removal of a Finance Minister who has been judged by many people to be incompetent; it was probably to remove an incompetent Energy Minister.
I want to speak for a moment on the National Energy policy as we are in a very interesting situation. The National Energy Program that was put forward in 1980 as a vehicle through which certain Government commitments were made proposed a number of key points: fair prices, fair treatment, security of supply. It went along for about a year and a half. The Government pushed through in a very vigorous manner Bill C-48, which was the legislative platform for that national energy policy; but by the time that Bill was part way through they found that they had to gut it. The Liberal Party, in concert, I would say, with the oil companies, gutted that Bill.
It moved forward again, but the basic assumptions in it were wrong. Then we had the national energy update in which it was admitted that revenue projections and certain activities were not going to be fulfilled; for instance, the collapse of the megaprojects. We found a situation where the economy would not benefit during this period from the National Energy Program, that revenue projections were not going to be sustained, and basically the assumptions and the circumstances upon which that program was built had changed and were in fact no longer appropriate. Therefore the Government was forced to change it.
We are in a situation today where we can point to numerous situations that have changed again. The recent decision of the National Energy Board approved very large exports of natural gas to the United States in the face of the Americans attempting to force down the price of gas. Essentially we are going to give away the resource in order to try and get some kind of cash flow going.
The Government came up with a proposal to export 40,000 barrels of light crude. Members of Parliament were told that we had 900 years' supply of oil and, therefore, could export it at almost any price. Very shortly after that we moved into a situation where we were told by the same oil companies that the projections they had made were wrong, that there was a very short supply and, therefore, we should put the price up.
We are now faced with the same kind of situation. The oil companies say that we have a surplus of oil in the Western Basin, that we should export that oil, but in fact we have a long-term shortness of supply so we should jack up the price to the world price. We have the Minister saying today in a waffling, mealy-mouth way that he intends to bow down to blackmail from the oil companies and pressure from the Provinces. They will no longer live up to their commitment to maintain a blended price for Canadian oil below the world price based on the old oil 75 per cent of world price.
We have a situation where the Government is backing away from firm commitments. It has seen the megaprojects collapse. It is trying to pump as much cheap gas as it can into the United States in order to bail themselves out. A very poor decision. We have a situation where we are again exporting

light crude. A week ago Thursday the Minister said in Vancouver that they are reviewing the whole matter of a natural gas pipeline to Vancouver Island. The main point is that the National Energy Program has collapsed. The National Energy Program update has collapsed. There is no doubt that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) must be pulling out his hair wondering where he will get all the money to fund the deficit and fund Government programs which are being strained to the nth degree. The Government made some very wrong projections on the economy. It made all the wrong projections on the source of revenue for energy. Because of the entire depressed nature of the economy, revenues are away down. However, demands continue for basic social institutions, health programs, Unemployment Insurance and income-support mechanisms. There are certainly difficulties in those areas. By and large it is based on incompetence.
It is unfortunate because the Government had a choice over the years to develop a broadly based industrial strategy in this country, but it failed to do so. It had a chance to strengthen our manufacturing sector to ensure that Canadians, instead of the Japanese and Europeans, use our raw resources and would realize the employment benefits from the value added. This has been a disaster in our forest industry where the Government has failed to act in an appropriate manner. It has not acted in an effective manner in the shipbuilding industry. and their Leader who crawled into bed with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on the Constitution. The two Parties are head to head, cheek to cheek, toe to toe and knee to knee. I am going no further because there are certain standards of decency which are observed in this Chamber. So the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River was saved from a lot of embarrassment.
When these nits get on the back of our legs we take up the other leg and give a little flick and the nit or the flea goes back to its accustomed spot, which is where the NDP are going after the next election. They are very much interested in the leadership of our Party. We have had many marvellous Leaders and we may have many more marvellous Leaders, but I am too modest, Mr. Speaker, to pursue that theme.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) spoke in this debate and he is certainly a good example of a man with his mind open at both ends. His mind is completely open and the wind whistles through the hollow space. He did not deal with the motion at all. The motion deals with the Government's repudiation of its 1980 election promises, and I will back that statement up. The motion deals with the question: Has the Government a mandate when it has completely turned its back on its solemn promises to the Canadian people and has operated now for three years in direct contravention of what it told the public?
We have all seen in the last three years what the Prime Minister stands for. He stands for whatever he thinks the public will fall for. We saw this here this morning in Question Period, with the Prime Minister trying to make believe that there is no moral crisis afflicting his Government in the area of the conflict of interest guidelines. As long as he thinks the people will fall for his explanations, no matter how specious, he will put them forward, and about the worst advice I can give him is to be himself and to keep on being himself.
What was the public asked to give the Liberal Party a mandate for in the last election? There is not too much evidence of what they were asked to do by the Liberal Party, or of the promises the Liberals made, because they did not make all that many promises. However, unwisely on January 12, 1980, the Prime Minister, who was then the Leader of the Opposition, the Leader of the Liberal Party, spoke in Toronto at a Liberal campaign college. None of them graduated because going to college has not helped them much, except to win elections. At this particular college, he outlined the platform of the Party to 500 Liberal candidates, campaign managers and Party workers from Ontario. After outlining his platform, he said, and I quote:
It would be the height of irresponsibility for any Party to make promises in the heat of an election campaign that could not be acted upon.
That is a very fine sentiment, of course. We, of course, completely agree with. It would be very irresponsible for him to do that. But what promises did he in fact make? He went on to say this, before he outlined the five themes which persuaded the Canadian people to vote for him, and I quote:
There is a prior commitment that I want to make clear. Liberals will do what we say we will do. And if we can't do it, we won't say it.

That was a revolutionary departure for these poor cretins at that policy conference to take in. They had never heard that before. But this is what the Prime Minister said:
Liberals will do what we say we will do. And if we can't do it, we won't say it.
Let us see if they did what they said. Have they observed the mandate they were supposed to have had? The Prime Minister also said, and I quote:
Our program for the 1980s consists of five major commitments:
The first commitment is, and I quote:
-to manage more rigorously the nation's finances in order to make more effective use of the taxpayers' money.
Has the Government met that major commitment? Between January, 1980 and now, what have the increases been in Government spending? In the year 1979-80 when the Prime Minister made that promise, the public accounts spending was $50.4 billion. This year it is going to be at least $80.4 billion. That is an additional $30 billion of spending. Is that managing more rigorously the nation's finances?
The deficit in the year 1979-80 was $11.4 billion. That was bad enough. It was a large deficit. It was the twelfth we had had in a row. But this year it is going to be $27.2 billion; that is almost two and a half times as much. When the Prime Minister promised to manage more rigorously our finances and to make more effective use of the taxpayers' money, our interest costs in that year were $8.3 billion. This year they are going to spend in excess of $17 billion. That is double. Is that managing the public money more rigorously? Is it making more effective use of the taxpayers' money when the interest bill is doubled in three years. This year $17 billion is being spent which does the public no good at all. It is just paying interest on the past debt. That was the first major commitment, and we can see from what I have said that it was completely broken.
Second, the Prime Minister said-and this is how he got into office-"We are going to achieve energy security at a fair price for all Canadians". Has he achieved energy security? Only in the sense that this year there is a greater supply of oil in the world than demand because of the fantastic recession we have had, but not in any other way. The tarsands plant and the Alsands plant have not gone ahead. The Cold Lake heavy oil plant has not gone ahead. The Beaufort Sea project is stumbling along. The Hibernia oil field off Newfoundland is just bumbling along because of the Government's greed and refusal to give the Province of Newfoundland a fair deal. And on and on it goes. We have had no increase in energy security.
By the way, in connection with that particular main plank of his platform, the Prime Minister also said this on February 12, 1980, and I quote:
The Liberal price hike would be less than half of what the Tories plan to inflict on you; we will negotiate an increase of less than 14 cents.
That is 14 cents a gallon. That was a deception beyond all deceptions, Mr. Speaker, because the public knows what has happened to oil and gas prices since the Prime Minister made that promise. In December, 1979 gasoline was selling at $1.14

a gallon. In December, 1982 gasoline was selling at $2.15 a gallon. The price has doubled.
In our budget, Mr. Speaker, we did not impose any tax on heating oil because we know the lower-income people generally use oil for heating. We know the Atlantic Provinces are heavily dependent on heating oil. The infamous 18-cent tax did not apply to heating oil at all, only to transportation fuels. But what has this Government done to help the lower-income Canadian on heating oil? Why, it was 70 cents a gallon in December, 1979 and it is $1.40 today. That is an increase of 70 cents a gallon, double the price. That is what this Government did to give Canadians energy security at a fair price. The Liberals have gouged them in every way you could conceive on energy prices. They have imposed more taxes than one could even dream of. Most of those increases are in federal Government taxes.
That was the second great plank of the Government's platform. Then, of course, the Prime Minister's third great policy was to develop, and I quote:
... industrial policies that will provide jobs, spur growth and increase Canadian ownership and control of the economy.
Well, in regard to that latter bit about increasing Canadian ownership and control, the Government has increased our ownership in the oil and gas industry minimally but at a cost to Canadians of interest rates that went sky high because of the Government's new energy policy and its anti-American rhetoric and the rest of it. It cost Canadians tens of billions of dollars in unnecessary interest rates to do that. But what is the good of Canadians owning our economy when the economy is diminishing, not growing? What price Canadian ownership then?
Well, Mr. Speaker, what about the industrial policies that will provide jobs? Do you know, Mr. Speaker-and this is why the Government should resign today-what has happened with jobs under this Government since it came into office just three years ago? We have added to the unemployment rolls 652,000 people. In January, 1980, there were 949,000 Canadians unemployed. As a result of three years of this Government, with the promises it made to provide jobs, the official rate is now 1,598,000 unemployed, an increase of 652,000. That is
652,000	Canadian families betrayed by this Government which promised it was going to develop industrial policies to provide jobs and spur growth. Spur growth, Mr. Speaker? Last year the Gross National Product went down 5 per cent. In other words, we Canadians, have 5 per cent less to share among ourselves this year than we had a year ago. Our Gross National Product did not increase, it did not stay the same, it went down 5 per cent last year. That is called spurring growth. In addition, there has been a net loss of jobs since the summer of 1981, just 16 or 18 months ago. We have lost 578,000 jobs in Canada. Is that spurring growth? Is that the industrial policy which will provide jobs? Surely to God, Mr. Speaker, this is a total betrayal of this Government's commitment to the Canadian people.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the public might think to themselves: could there be any further betrayals of our interest? Why, yes, there certainly are further betrayals because the Prime Minister at the same meeting said this:
We must endorse the right of every Canadian to have a job.
That is what that monumental mountebank, that hypocrite who now leads this country said, and I quote him again:
We must endorse the right of every Canadian to have a job.
Well, there are 1,598,000 Canadians out there wondering what that means. What is the good to them of a Prime Minister who endorses the right to have a job and then does nothing to keep his promise? The hypocrite!
The fourth plank in that program, Mr. Speaker.
To build greater economic strength in each region of the country as the basis for over-all Canadian prosperity.
Well, Canada is devastated from coast to coast. British Columbia, one of the most booming regions of Canada, has been devastated in the last several years. It has almost as high an unemployment rate as Newfoundland. Newfoundland has been devastated even more than it was already by a Government which has done everything it can to inflict pain upon the Government and people of that Province by cutting back DREE spending and economic assistance, by doing everything it can to damage that Province because they want a fair deal on the offshore mineral resources. That is what this Government has done for the regions of this country.
The fifth great plank was this, Mr. Speaker, and this is the greatest betrayal of them all. I hope the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) will listen to me. He is supposed to be a man of some sensitivity but he is having his ears filled now with some specious nonsense by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). I want the Minister of Public Works to listen. This was the fifth plank in the Prime Minister's platform:
To enhance the security of the individual by helping those who most need assistance.
That was the solemn pledge to the Canadian people on January 12, 1980, by your Leader at the campaign college in Toronto. The Liberals were going to enhance the security of the invdividual by helping those who most need assistance. He went on to say this, Mr. Speaker:
And most important of all, we must guarantee the income security of our older citizens. Retirement should be a time of peace rather than a time of fear.
Can you hear the violins being played while the sanctimonious Prime Minister assured our older Canadians that retirement should be a time of peace rather than a time of fear? What did he do then? He led the Government which reduced indexing, which took away from the income this year of 1.1 million Old Age Security recipients. He put the boots to
200,000	Public Service pensioners. That is how the Government enhances the security of the individual. That is how it helps those who most need assistance. Well, who have the Liberals helped? Why, they have helped Alastair Gillespie. We have seen how the Prime Minister's heart was rended today for Alastair Gillespie. Poor Alastair was forced to the private
February 18, 1983

sector. The Prime Minister said here in the House today that poor Alastair had to go out and be like an ordinary Canadian and look for a job, "and we had to fix poor Alastair up." That was the implication. This Toronto industrialist, Alastair Gillespie, our hearts were supposed to cry for him when we have 1,598,000 people who the Prime Minister has not fixed up with some fancy deal through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) and the Acting Deputy Prime Minister; this sleazy, tawdry affair that we are exploring in this House today.
Let us pray.

The Liberals are going to enhance the security of the Liberals who are heaped upon the CMHC Board of Directors. It is not good enough that they should get $150 a day; their pay is going up to $450 a day. For Sylvia Sutherland, a defeated Liberal in Peterborough in the last election- that is her only qualification for being a director of CMHC- $150 a day was not good enough to attend meetings here in Ottawa; she has to get $450 a day.
Don't attack people who cannot defend themselves.

The retired President of CMHC, Mr. Hession, said that $450 a day was "pretty low" for directors of Crown Corporations. Imagine, pretty low! Yes, it is prettry low, low in the sense that it is pretty damn mean. It is pretty tawdry. It is a scoundrelly thing to do to give the directors of CMHC a 200 per cent increase and to reduce the incomes of old age pensioners and Public Service pensioners. That is who the Liberals are helping, their friends and pals. That is the security they are enhancing. Those are the people they think need assistance most. Donald Macdonald, the corporate lawyer from Toronto who is supposed to save the Liberal Party from Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Turner, is to get $850 a day on his Royal Commission. Why? Because poor McCarthy and McCarthy's overhead costs would go to hell if he did not get this from the public Treasury. This is the hero who is to save us from John Turner. This is the Party, Mr. Speaker, and I quote again, which will:
-not simply stand by and let the recession come. We will fight it and overcome it.
When are they going to start fighting and overcoming the recession? Ronald Reagan is going to pull us out of our recession temporarily, to some extent this year, but the Government of Canada has done nothing to pull us out of anything. The Prime Minister went on to say this:
All this we will do. And more. So that is our commitment.
Well, that is the point of our resolution today, Mr. Speaker. The Government has not met those commitments. It has repudiated those commitments. The Liberals have got themselves here in office and they have done nothing but roll in the trough. I said the Prime Minister's conduct today was hircine, it was goat-like. It had the smell of a goat when he attempted to defend the indefensible here today. The Liberals have become a coalition of looters, Mr. Speaker, despoilers, favour

seekers, patronage granters, patronage receivers, murky influence peddlars, jesuitical justifiers. Did anyone ever see such jesuitical twisting and turning, as we have seen the Prime Minister do in the last several days when he was trying to justify the immoral plundering of the public purse by the cutpurses of the twentieth century led by a dacoit who will defend anything his Ministers, his former Ministers or the Liberal Party associates will attempt to do.
That is why we have moved this motion, Mr. Speaker. It is not because we expect the Government to pay any attention or because we think there are millions watching this Chamber today, but because we want to have on record what we think of the disgraceful spectacle we face in this Chamber week after week, day after day and month after month.
I say to the Prime Minister that if he wants to give the people of Canada a chance to judge the conduct in the Lalonde-MacEachen scandal-the Maclonde scandal-let us have an election now. Let him call an election now. We do not need a leader in this Party to clean your clock in an election. We will bollix you. Give us six weeks and we will devastate you. We will wipe you out. You will be lucky to have a remnant left. Go to the public on your betrayal of your commitments and we will stun you into insensibility. You will not survive. There will be none of you here for the rest of the twentieth century, and it is just about time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and I think a good title for his speech would be: "Variations on an unfinished theme". I could not believe my ears, Mr. Speaker, here in the House of Commons, when, as the Hon. Member said earlier, millions of people might be watching the proceedings they probably seldom heard such arrant nonsense. It is very easy for the Opposition to say more or less what they like, except that when people have to make up their minds in a year or two, they will have to vote for the party they think is the most responsible, and if they remember this speech by the Member for St. John's West, I think it would make a rather peculiar impression during an election campaign. Imagine, a political party that says it does not need a leader and does not need ideas to be elected. Mr. Speaker, such a party would be disaster for this country.

February 18, 1983
