I would like to give some statistics on what has been done by this Government in the past three years, but first I would like to refer to the motion put by the Opposition party, which says, and I quote:
That, in light of the Government's outright betrayal of the Canadian people and its repudiation of its 1980 election promises to reduce unemployment, combat inflation, avoid inflationary tax hikes and excessive energy price increases, reduce the deficit, and implement an industrial strategy for Canada, this House calls upon the Government to face its responsibility to Canadians and take immediate action to live up to the commitments that it made in 1980 or resign.
Mr. Speaker, if I may draw a parallel between what was said earlier and what the situation is today, I would like to refer to what is happening in my riding in connection with the mining companies Iron Ore, Sidbec-Normine and Wabush Mines or else companies such as Quebec North Shore and others in the private sector that are having problems. If I wanted to see things in black and white, Mr. Speaker, as the Opposition preferred to do just now, I could say that Iron Ore's problems were brought about by its President, Mr. Brian Mulroney, a well-known figure whom I know very well and for whom I have a great deal of respect. But I will not follow the lead of the Opposition. I am not going to say that Iron Ore's problems were brought about by the President of Iron Ore. It is a matter of economics, and when they say that we have increased unemployment in this country, I could answer that unemployment in my area is due to Mr. Brian Mulroney, because we have a town that is about to disappear and people who have been laid off. It is very easy to make fancy speeches and say whatever comes to mind, under the cover of parliamentary immunity, without taking responsibility for one's statements. It is easy to indulge in crass rhetoric and to establish a relation of cause and effect between a weak economy and high unemployment, but I think that if we are to be the least bit reasonable and realistic, we must make comparisons that take the economic situation into account. I really deplore the fact that in the House, everything the Opposition says boils down to entirely haphazard discussions in which no connection is made with socio-economic questions and in which there is no rhyme or reason or logic. Instead of proposals and alternative solutions, there is only the same old refrain we have been hearing for well-nigh twenty years, which is that everything this Government has done badly, and that its decisions have always been the wrong decisions.
Mr. Speaker, this crass rhetoric is one reason why I am tempted to say that the Official Opposition may not be ready to form a new Government, because it has no real solutions to propose. All they do here in the House is repeat the same old thing, day in and day out.
Mr. Speaker, if we compare Canada's position to that of the United States, we see that all things being equal, Canada's public finances are in better shape than those of the U.S. If we examine the proposals made by Mr. Miterrand when he ran for office, these were measures to reduce unemployment, strengthen the franc and upgrade the industrial sector. Two
years later, France has record levels of inflation, record levels of unemployment and the value of the franc has plummeted.
The Official Opposition had all the answers. It is very easy to be in the Opposition and to say that if the Opposition were in power, it would settle most of the country's problems. In France, the former Opposition has been in power for nine months, and has done what it could during that time. There are no miracles. A responsible Government must tell the people that it cannot work miracles. But when I hear people say in the House that nothing at all has been done, well, if it is not rhetoric, it is very close to being a lie.
I would like to say a few words about expenditures that were made by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in 1981-82. For industrial expansion alone, which means in the private sector, grants totalled $98 million in 1980-81 and $119 million in 1981-82. Guaranteed loans totalled $231 million in 1980-81 and $131 million in 1982. In other words, the amount of money spent on grants to help private enterprise was greater than the amount spent on guaranteed loans. With respect to defence industries, Mr. Speaker, there were $142 million in
1980-	81 and $262 million in 1981-82; for the development of export markets, Mr. Speaker, $17 million in 1980-81 and $24 million in 1981-82; for shipbuilding and modernization, $102 million in 1980-81 and $143 million in 1981-82. The Opposition will note that the amounts have steadily increased.
For research and development in the field of energy, the amounts vary between $4 and $6 million for both years. For the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, $180 million in 1980-81 and $206 million in 1981-82. The Federal Business Development Bank was allowed $484 million in 198081 and $460 million in 1981-82. The National Research Council obtained $3 million in 1980-81 and $4 million in
1981-	82. The grand total, Mr. Speaker, is $5,234 million in 1980-81 and $8,189 million in 1981-82.
Of course, if we went into details, we would realize that some positive achievements were made. The Official Opposition should recognize those facts and suggest whatever should be done to extend the effects of such fundings. We would be interested in hearing such suggestions from the Official Opposition, but we never do. And this is what Canadians would like to hear. What are the proposals brought forward by the Official Opposition. We would like to compare them with our government policies so that a better choice may be made. Such is the advantage of democratic debates: we know exactly what is going on so that the best choice can be made advisedly. It is too bad but the Hon. members opposite have never heard about alternatives.
To give still further facts which are not only related to figures, we could point out some plans and complementary agreements signed since 1978 but I will only go back to 1980. I will give you an exemple in Quebec and in Ontario. In Quebec, under an agreement signed on June 20, 1981, with respect to
February 18, 1983

the development of transport, the federal government will pay $3,600,000; for forest development, $110,400,000. Some $24 million to promote the tourist industry, $105 million to upgrade the pulp and paper industry, $25.5 million from the Federal Government to build a newspaper mill in Amos, $5.5 million for Quebec's Societe Interport, $60 million to modernize pulp and paper mills in Ontario, $33 million for eastern Ontario, $10 million for rural development in northern regions, and $21 million for Sault Sainte Marie's infrastructure. I wish I had enough time to give concrete examples of what is being done by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to help our industries become more competitive and put our private sector on a sound basis. It is very important for our private sector to operate on a self-supporting basis, for it will then be able to seek ever expanding export markets, create more jobs and generate revenues to pave the way towards better days for the Government and all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, in the Drummondville area, the Soprema Company has just announced a $3.7 million investment in a roof sheeting plant. It is an international company based in France and it will receive a $1 million grant from the Federal Government.
What I find astounding in this debate, Mr. Speaker, is the bad faith of Members opposite. When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister or Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lumley) signed the most important contract for the private sector of Canada, the Bombardier contract, the Progressive Conservative Party raised objections about the way the Canadian Government had awarded the contract. Our Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce deserves praise for taking calculated risks with a view to landing that contract. We all know that even the Americans were extremely shocked and critical about the way we had managed this deal, but still we did succeed in keeping the contract and getting people back to work. When it was announced that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, through the Minister, had just signed the contract, Hon. Members on the other side raised hell about it. And yet, that is the best example of a Government which has made a significant contribution by signing that agreement; we will now be able to make progress in the field of new technology and open up new markets while competing against countries such as France and Japan. That is what counts, but Members opposite cannot find anything constructive to say about it.
Perhaps they should stop making empty speeches and give us more logical and more responsible arguments, and indeed tell us just what they would do if they were on this side. I would also like Members of the Opposition to tell us whether they would have signed the Bombardier contract if they had been in office. Yes or no, Mr. Speaker, would they have given jobs to the people in the regions of Montmagny-L'Islet and Valcourt? Or would they have helped promote the establishment of a new technology in the United States? I hope they will give me an answer to that because I think it is important.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for St. John's West should have remained in the House to follow the debate on this important issue of fisheries. During the three years I have been a Member of this House, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has made wonders for Eastern Quebec and Eastern Canada, streamlining all our infrastructures, making it possible for our fishermen who live far away from the national capital to benefit from capital investments and thus compete on world markets with such countries as Norway, Finland and Sweden. That was something important that we felt we had to do and which we have done. Moreover, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) announced yesterday a $200 million investment plan to update the fisheries, without waiting for the opposition to move a non confidence motion. So much so that the Kirby report which was made public yesterday contains the Task Force's 57 recommendations to improve the industry so that it may expand considerably and use advanced technology to compete with other countries.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that any sincere person would realize that these are positive steps on the part of the Government, and should stop repeating in the House platitudes and vain arguments. It would be nice, for a change, to hear from opposition members a non-biased and rational debate, as well as suggestions to improve the situation. What is lacking most in the House, Mr. Speaker, are new and creative ideas. That's what is missing! They rely on the Government to take action, and they never have any new initiative or solution to put forward.
Mr. Speaker, it is important to note what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has done over the last three years to rationalize the sea, air and rail transport operations within his Department. Let us look at what is happening to Interports in Montreal and the corporation of the Old Port in Quebec City. Projects worth millions of dollars have been initiated in both cities, and they are being funded either by the federal government alone or else in a proportion of 60 to 40 p. 100 by the federal government and the Province of Quebec. I shall just mention the Centre des Congres.
We can boast of outstanding achievements, Mr. Speaker but readily admit that the present economic situation is difficult for everyone. Yet, compared to other countries, Canada is doing quite well in the middle term. It is true that the Canadian dollar is weak compared with the American dollar, but we should perhaps be telling Canadians that our dollar is now at its real value, except that in relation to the French franc, the British pound or the German mark, our dollar is very strong on European markets. We must realize it. We should stop cultivating our guilt complex and our negativism, because we are doing well in certain areas, but tend to look only at our failures. Talking about our successes, Mr. Speaker, I should perhaps add for the benefit of the Opposition that we are now merging the operations of the former Department of Regional Economic Expansion with the Department of Industry, Trade

February 18, 1983

and Commerce into one large Department to ensure a better regional presence so that we may help small and medium-size businesses and provide assistance to those who want to expand their present business. Mr. Speaker, there soon will be before the House a bill merging these two Departments, and I hope that we shall have the support or at least the views of the Opposition on this matter and that their proposals or additional ideas will help make our proposal even better. The merging of these two Departments is an important step in the Canadian government's efforts to provide assistance to various kinds of businesses.
Mr. Speaker, I know that our time is very short, and realising that the oppositions motion aims at asking for the Government's resignation or calling an election, I wish to point out that we certainly have an unemployment problem, but as I said earlier, we cannot blame the situation on the Government, just as I would not blame the board of directors of certain companies in my region. It is quite wrong to say that the Government has no industrial strategy as we shall see when the Government introduces a complete revision of our industrial legislation in the very near future. The Members opposite say that inflation is rising, Mr. Speaker, but I believe that is because they have not seen the latest figures. We are fighting inflation and all of us, as Canadians, shall win that fight. In the last three months, the price index has gone down and inflation has shown obvious signs of weakening.
As for interest rates, Mr. Speaker, we see that the bank rate has already gone down to 9.5 per cent, which puts the mortgage rate at 11.5 per cent, while these same rates were reaching 18 and 20 per cent one year ago. These are very encouraging signs, Mr. Speaker, and the Opposition had better have another look at the figures they quoted, and try to understand them.
Mr. Speaker, I invite the Opposition Members to show much more creativity and responsibility, and any solution they may suggest in this House would be greatly appreciated because Canadians have no use for people who cry over spilt milk, what they need are people who can suggest solutions or provide answers.

Mr. Speaker, I should respond directly and immediately to some of the comments of the previous speaker. Our motion is intended to take the form of a report card on the Government's record on the third anniversary of its election.
The Hon. Member's defence of the Government's record over the last three years does not refute any of the items in the motion. He did not make any reference to the items that the Government promised to deliver, nor has he in any way indicated that the Government has delivered on those promises. The consistent response from the other side is that they want to hear what the Opposition would do if we were in their place. Those Members do hear what the Opposition would do
if it was the Government. Various Members from this side, including the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) and others, do make suggestions to the Government when we are debating economic issues. Therefore, I suggest that the Hon. Member is wrong in his analysis. The purpose of this motion is to indicate that this Party had the courage to go to the people in 1980 and tell them precisely what needed to be done in this country in economic terms. Members opposite went to the people and said different things, I believe. The Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher), a Liberal on the other side, is even shaking his head at that statement. I take it that what he is saying is that the Liberals went to the people and told them the same things that we did. That clearly is not true.
Liberals clearly told the people different things from what we said. But let me remind the Member from Mississauga North of some of the promises that the Liberals made. The question for debate today is surely not what this Party would do if it was in power today. That is a matter that will be debated on other days when there are economic policy projections discussed in the House. It is a matter that will be debated in the next election. The Hon. Member knows that. The question for today, three years after their election, is whether the Government has delivered on the promises it made in the election campaign. It is no defence for the Liberal Government to attempt to explain what it has done by telling us about all the money it has given to people.
Spent.

The money it has spent. That is in fact proof that the claim the Liberal Government made that it would exercise fiscal restraint has not been honoured.
Canadians are becoming increasingly aware that the country cannot be put back to work simply by having the Government take more money from the private sector or anywhere else and spending it on job creation programs, however well intended. There is a trend line which Members opposite have to face. Every year that the deficit goes up, unemployment goes up in lock step with it. There is a relationship between those two facts. Simply, the more money one takes from the system where it is being spent efficiently and puts into the bureaucracy for however well intentioned programs, the greater the loss to the national system. The pursuit of that policy will only result in more unemployment.
The Government cannot defend its failure to keep its promises by talking about what it has spent its money on. I do not think that is what the electorate really believed when they swallowed this. Creating opportunities to go on Unemployment Insurance?
The third offer was to provide security. Security of what kind? I do not know whether you are aware, Mr. Speaker, that since that particular time the growth of bank deposits in savings accounts has risen at an extraordinary rate. If I can quote from the National Finances published by the Canadian Tax Foundation for 1981-82, in 1979, the amount of personal savings have increased from about $30 billion in 1979 to about $80 billion today. That is not a reflection of economic security, that is fear. The general public does not know where it can, with confidence and security, place its funds.
At one time it was thought possible that if you had money to invest, you could invest it in the energy field. I do not know whether you have been following the trends in the energy field on the stock market, Mr. Speaker, but there are only one or two companies going in the right direction. Dome has gone down, and there are a good number of others. There are a number of loyal Canadians who would like to be able to invest in their country.
This was not a public undertaking to provide security, but it was an undertaking given to candidates and they went out and said, "Don't you worry, we will provide security." What has the Government done? It has squandered the revenue of this country in a manner which has never been seen before. This statement I have been reading from goes on to say that the program for 1980 consists of five major commitments. One was to manage more rigorously the nation's finances in order to make more effective use of taxpayers' money. Well, what were we debating yesterday, Mr. Speaker? We were debating a Bill to authorize this Government to borrow $19 billion. Now, I do not know whether this Bill has ever been contested
February 18, 1983

by the Chair as being an omnibus Bill and it should therefore be split up into two different Bills, one for the 1982-83 year, and the other for borrowings for next year. That is a possibility. It ought not to be presented in this form. Nonetheless, $19 billion is being sought. I wish I could find the figures on the borrowing. They are around somewhere amongst all these papers, but I would say it is something of the order of $45 billion to $50 billion which this Government has sought to borrow in this Parliament, while at the same time making the statement that it would manage more rigorously the nation's finances.
Over three years? Come on.

In three years. I now come to the commitment to achieve energy security at a fair price. The figure which comes to mind on the purchase by PetroCan of Petrofina is about $1.5 billion. That is part of the debt that your children and mine have to pay down the road, $1.5 billion to acquire a series of storefronts to match those acquired earlier for a somewhat smaller sum on the West Coast through the purchase of Pacific Petroleum. All the Petrofina stations have been repainted, and it cost $1.5 billion to repaint them, put up the signs, the Maple Leaf, and everything. But not one drop of new petroleum resources was acquired in that purchase, Mr. Speaker. Just the storefront, that is all. This is the manner in which you achieve energy security at a fair price. Fair price, Mr. Speaker? We find that in December, 1979, when that infamous resolution was passed down here-
You mean the day you could not count?

I was here. In December, 1979 we were paying 24.6 cents a litre for gasoline at the pump. That translates into a language which other people understand as $1.12 a gallon. Well, today, in Ottawa, it is about 42 cents or 43 cents a litre for regular.
It is 43.3 cents.

All right, 43.3. So we have an increase of 18 cents. Now, that is odd, is it not? Eighteen cents a litre. I remember hearing something about 18 cents a gallon at one particular time, and now we find it has gone up 18 cents a litre. Now, where are we? The national average was 25 cents a litre in December of 1979 and it is 47 cents a litre in September of 1982. I guess we get into the 18 cents business there, too. Rather strange. That is 22 cents a litre more on average.
I really wonder how these gullible people could have been soaked in by these promises-the promises about which we are speaking today-the promises that have been repudiated.
The fourth commitment was to develop an industrial policy that will provide jobs. Jobs for whom? For the Japanese? If we look at the statistics for unemployment in 1979 we would see how they were going to provide jobs. At that time 838,000
Supply
Canadians were out of work. Today, Mr. Speaker, at least
1,600,000	are out of work. Is that what they call providing jobs? The only way the Government seems to be able to provide jobs is to throw money around.
The Liberals were going to build greater economic strength in each region. I should like to give you some figures for the amounts of money that has been poured into the various Provinces through the Regional Development Incentives Programs. Newfoundland got $30 million; Prince Edward Island, $22 million; Nova Scotia, $79.8 million; New Brunswick, $81.2 million; Quebec, $530.1 million; Ontario, $94.7 million; Manitoba, $100 million; Saskatchewan, $33.6 million; Alberta, $35.3 million; British Columbia, $10.8 million; and Yukon, $0.4 million, for a total of $1 billion. That is since 1970, Mr. Speaker. Those figures hardly fit the promise to build greater economic strength into each region of the country as a basis for over-all prosperity.
The fifth undertaking was to enhance security of the individual by helping those who most need assistance. In last week's debate we heard what happened about that. The pensioners found that their pension cheques have been reduced from the undertaking that was given them to index to the CPI; instead they must conform with the six and five program.
What about GIS?

The GIS was left alone. The indexing of public servants' pensions was also reduced to conform with the six and five formula. Is that the best we can do for the security of the individual, to help those who most need assistance?

In light of his concern for the same people, could he tell us why his Party deliberately refused to extend debate on the income tax legislation last Monday night when we wanted to get that legislation through?

Excuse the outburst, Mr. Speaker, but with all due respect I feel that it was necessary to use an expletive like that. The income tax forms for the collection of income tax ought to be before the House in January or even in December.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the Hon. Member that those tax measures were introduced in November, 1981 and more were brought in in June, 1982. The Finance Committee met to discuss them in the fall of 1982, and there has been extended debate both in public and in this Chamber, on those measures.

Why did his Party refuse to speed up debate so that we could legally mail refunds to those people who need them the most?

Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand why the Government did not bring in that measure earlier. I suppose it is difficult to bring in income tax measures until they decide how much the deficit will be. In November 1981 it was $13.3 billion and now it is $27.2 billion. They cannot make up their minds how much the deficit is going to be, let alone what measures apply to income tax.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to my good friend, the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich. I should like to tell him that one of the three people watching is my grandmother, and first he should restrain his expletives in response to my question.
He said he remembered the time when gas was 18 cents a gallon. Many of us remember that. I wonder if he also remembers and will put on record-and if he cannot, I can-that in the budget brought in by the former Minister of Finance, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), one of the appendices clearly sets forth a pricing schedule, which would have meant that gasoline prices and heating fuel prices at the pump in 1983 would be higher than they actually are at present.
Would the Hon. Member respond to that question without expletives?

Mr, Speaker, I apologize to the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) for having used a word with which he was not familiar.
I would be very pleased if the Hon. Member would send to me in the mail-and not by Canada Post, please, because it might take too long-a copy of this particular fabrication.

Of course I will do so, Mr. Speaker. Not tomorrow but on Monday. The Hon. Member has waited three years without reading the information, so I am sure he can wait another 48 hours or so. I will also send it to the people in my riding through my Householder. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I explain a difficulty. It is often a courtesy to recognize an Hon. Member from the same Party by which the motion under debate was originally put forward so that it might be given the opportunity to complete debate before the end of the day. However, another tradition is that ordinarily we alternate speakers between left and right. Under the circumstances and unless I hear some other proposition, I would have to recognize the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans).

Mr. Speaker, in a sense of fairness to the tradition I would be prepared to stop at ten minutes to five and split the time with the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta).
I have a few things to say about the motion before the House. I would like to look at the situation which faces us and at the options which are available to the Government to try to assess what it is that we are up against and why, in light of that, I think the motion is totally and wholly out of order.
We have been told on a number of occasions-and 1 firmly believe Canadians have come to realize it-that the economic disorders of the country are not solely those of Canada, and that the economic situation which Canadians are experiencing is not solely the responsibility of Canadians. We are an export nation. We depend very heavily for our Gross National Product, for our national income and for our livelihoods, on our ability to sell. What we have sold the most and sold best has been natural resources and the processed materials from them. It is well known on the West Coast that the lumber industry or the forest products industry is suffering, not as a result of policies of the federal Government or of provincial Governments, but as a result of the fact that these products cannot be sold in foreign markets. Also the mining industry is suffering today, not as a result of policies of the federal Government or provincial Governments, but as a result of the fact that we cannot sell nickel or iron ore in world markets because the markets do not exist as a result of world recession.
The same conditions, to a greater or lesser degree, as we are experiencing in Canada are being experienced by every western industrialized nation in the world. It does absolutely nothing for the psychology or understanding of Canadians for the Opposition to put forward a motion which inappropriately and falsely lays the entire blame on Government or Governments in this country for the economic situation we face. We certainly have a role to play. I defy Hon. Members opposite to say that the Government is not doing in a positive way everything within its means to resolve the problems we are facing.
We can trace the difficulties back for many years in all western industrialized economies. We were told in the 1970s that inflation had to be brought down. In fact, the Opposition demanded that inflation be brought down. It realizes, as we
February 18, 1983

realize, that if we let inflation get out of control, it creates massive uncertainty, cuts back on investment, reduces economic growth and drives up interest rates in the system. These kinds of conditions are not conducive to rising standards of living or being able to maintain present standards. For example, in 1975 Government policy implemented through the Bank of Canada began to restrain the economy or to do something about the inflationary problem. Other countries have followed suit with precisely the same policy because it was the only way to deal with the inflationary problem.
Inflation is simple. It is too much purchasing power chasing too few goods and not enough economic output. In this situation prices rise, and we have a productivity problem and an output problem. This is inflation.
Under a standard economic arrangement where markets are free to adjust, which does not exist in this country, United States, France or Germany-but it does exist in Japan to a certain extent-when demand falls, the incomes of all people in society would fall somewhat to reduce their incomes in line with the demand in order to combat inflation or to bring demand into line with output. This would stop inflation, but we have a system in which there are a great many rigidities and structural problems with labour-management relations and the way we do business in the country, privately, governmentally and otherwise. Our system adjusts to a reduction in demand. The only way to solve inflation is to reduce demand, so that we quit putting upward pressures on prices. The way our system adjusts to that kind of situation is that it leaves the majority of people with the high incomes they had prior to the fight against inflation and throws other people out of work. We have a compensation system in Canada which yields precisely that result. When recession hits, when demand falls, the majority keep their incomes and remain stable. It has no impact on their standard of living, but the minority gets thrown out on the street. This is the way our system works. I do not think that is how it should work.
The Japanese compensation system provides for greater flexibility of wages in management and labour, so that everyone shares in the income loss somewhat but no one suffers a dramatic decline in their standard of living. Our system does not operate that way. It operates in the manner I have described, and we see 1.5 million people thrown out of work. This is the way our system responds to the fight against inflation, which is necessary.
There is only one method of handling it. If we do not believe that the people thrown out of work should be asked to bear the entire brunt of a recession, or a fight against inflation, then governments have a responsibility, which all of us have recognized, to ensure that there is a social safety net to ratch these people before they are left destitute. We have done that in Canada. I might add, in a non-partisan spirit, that this has been done by past Liberal Governments with the introduction of unemployment insurance, welfare programs, medicare and pensions, all designed to cushion people affected by the adjustment process I have just described.
Supply
We are faced with a situation that is real. We know what it is. Also we are faced with some very real options. The Government can respond to this problem by reinflating the economy; in other words, printing more money, selling bonds to the Bank of Canada, taking that money and spending it, investing it, or giving it to people to ensure that their incomes remain above a minimal level. This would generate inflation again, and we would be right back into the same cycle. Also, the Government can increase taxes on those people who continue to have jobs in order to provide the funds necessary to subsidize those who do not have jobs. This is possible.
If we did that today, we would probably drive the economy further into recession because we would reduce the incentives to produce and grow. That is not a possible option. The only other option left to a Government faced with an economy in which the psychology is so badly shaken that individuals will not invest on their own and consumers are saving at high rates, is the classics Keynesian one-the Government borrows funds from the public and puts them into the marketplace to stimulate demand, or it can put those funds into the hands of individuals who are out of work and suffering, and let the deficit rise.
The Opposition screams that the deficit is out of control. There are many ways of analysing the deficit. Some people at the University of Toronto and in other places have analysed the situation and made a distinction between the structural and the entire deficit, that during a serious major economic downturn, deficits should rise; but just as true, during times of economic expansion, deficits must be reduced. I suggest that in this period of time, when deficits have risen, it is exactly what should happen in a society that has a system like ours and that adjusts like ours if we are not to allow people to become destitute, re-ignite the fires of inflation and raise the taxes to the extent that it will drive the economy further away from growth.
Effectively, we are running a deficit now because we are borrowing against the future. Deficits are tax liabilities for the future. Those deficits are justified and the actions are correct if they are incurred to invest in the future and to generate greater income for the future and provide more jobs for the future. That is precisely what the Government is trying to do with the deficit. We are trying to invest in capital infrastructure and in human capital through the skills and training programs. We are trying to invest and expand the potential of people and capital for the future which will generate the income and allow us to reduce the deficits.
Let me just say that we certainly have achieved some of our objectives and we will achieve more. We will achieve the objective of reducing unemployment. Finally, with respect to inflation, as of today it is down to 8.3 per cent. If you look at what inflation has been over the last six months on an annualized basis, it is 4.6 per cent. Annualized for the last three months, November, December and January, the inflation rate in Canada is running at 2.2 per cent. Inflation has come down. This is an achievement which will help bring down interest

rates and stimulate the economic growth, and that is how we will attack the unemployment problem.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by saying that I appreciate the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) relinquishing part of his time so I may participate and wrap up this debate this afternoon. I would also like to congratulate him on his speech. It was certainly one of the better speeches that was made this afternoon. Certainly, many people would agree with the general theme of his remarks.
I would say, however, that one of the things he obviously did not mention-probably because of lack of time-is that inflation is primarily caused by governments. The Government has shown its record for creating inflation. Obviously, we cannot insulate ourselves from world recession which has taken place, but the Government has played a major role in our experiencing higher inflation than necessary. That is what concerns Canadians the most at this time.
The National Energy Program is a good example of Government mismanagement which has caused a tremendous amount of money to leave the country.
The Hon. Member also failed to mention the fact that the economy has just not performed. The Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development, OECD, indicated in its 1982 estimates that Canada's real economic growth performance was the worst of any country in the industrialized world. Our growth as a percentage of GNP was minus 5 per cent. This is clearly part of the problem. The Government could obviously have played a geat role in this area but has not done so. Canada's performance was behind the performance of countries such as Iceland, Sweden, The Netherlands, Luxembourg, Greece, Portugal and Turkey. Surely the Government must take some responsibility for the economic mess we are in when one sees these figures. These figures are given to us by what must be considered an independent and objective body that examines 24 countries in the world. It found Canada to be at the bottom, twenty-fourth.
Canada has a history of being a great democracy. It is probably one of the greatest in the world. Democracy involves free elections and people expressing their opinion in an election campaign.
Mr. Speaker, I will make my point of order very brief.
Sit down.
I recognize that the Hon. Member has very limited time. Since there will be no time for questions, I wonder if he would permit a brief question.
Sit down.

Before the interruption, Mr. Speaker, I was saying that Canada is a great democracy in which people are elected after telling their voters what they intend to do if elected. The motion that we are debating today results from the 1980 election campaign. During that campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and the country, knowing full well that we were entering a recession, made to the people a series of statements that were as far from the truth as could be imagined.
One statement the Prime Minister made was, "This Party will not simply stand by and let the recession come." Obviously, the Prime Minister knew the recession was coming. He also said, "We will fight it and overcome it". He went on to say that the Liberals would fight to lower unemployment when the Conservatives planned to increase unemployment by 100,000 people. When he knew the recession was coming, he made a statement like that.
At the present time, in January of 1983, the unemployment rate is 12.4 per cent. In January of 1980, it was 7.5 per cent. At the present time we have some 1,598,000, almost 1.6 million Canadians out of work. That is some 650,000 more than in January, 1980.
It was statements like that that have been discussed today. The Prime Minister, knowing full well what would happen and that this country was possibly entering a severe recession which would make times much worse, purposely neglected to tell the Canadian people what was to happen. In effect, he sugar coated the pill for the Canadian people. Unfortunately, they swallowed it and elected the present Government.
That is what this debate is really all about. Unless the Government owns up and tries in a meaningful way-much in the way the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre indicated-to deal with the economy in a sensible fashion, not only will the Liberal Party be hurt by its statements, the whole democratic process of the country will be in jeopardy. People just do not believe what politicians say any more. I thank Hon. Members for their indulgence and I will bring this debate to an end.
